requirements.statement: The tests repo's visual-regression suite guards rendered composition: layout, spacing, colour and typography as the user sees a page, by comparing screenshots against committed baselines and failing when pixels differ outside the masked regions. Every spec carries the @visual tag and forces a headless browser for itself, because headed mode uses the operating system's own font rendering; on macOS the browser is launched with always-shown scroll bars and a coarse pointer so a Mac shot matches the Linux baseline. Each shot is committed twice, once for each platform, and both are regenerated when a visual change is intended, the Linux ones from a container that reaches the stack by its host name; regeneration can be narrowed to one spec or title, or write only missing baselines. A shot is taken at 1280 by 1000 pixels unless the test resizes the viewport. Content that moves with the clock or the run is pinned: a full-page shot of a notification page masks the whole status strip rather than the reference alone, so the masked box stays a fixed size, while the notification view and declaration shots overwrite the reference number and the dates with fixed text; a calendar shot stops the browser clock on a fixed day and moves the served earliest and latest dates by the same number of days. Only the animals and plants domains have visual specs.
requirements.why: A change to shared page chrome is exactly what this suite exists to catch, so every chrome change either keeps the baselines or regenerates both platforms' baselines in the same increment.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p11-001 to p11-010 and p16-096 to p16-105 define the suite, its dual baselines, its headless and macOS rules, its viewport and its masks; repo-tests-p16-102 and p16-102-m1 give the regeneration commands and how to narrow them.

requirements.statement: Which pages and states the visual suite pins, and its coverage gaps, are weighed where those pages are weighed: the origin page on first load and with its region code revealed, the import reason page in its transhipment, transit, temporary admission, error and no-JavaScript states, the arrival details page, the transited countries page empty and with one country, the identification card, the accompanying documents page with one scanned document, the consignor picker's search row, the arrival date picker's button at rest, hovered and focused and its calendar opened by mouse and by keyboard, the overview's totals, the notification view of a ready draft at desktop width down to the Consignment addresses card, the refused review at desktop and phone width and the declaration. No baseline covers the germinal-products set, the notification list, the confirmation page, the commodity pages, the address book or the INS front door, and the review has a desktop baseline but no phone one.
requirements.why: Each baseline pins one page's own composition, so the page's area weighs it against the target design; the missing baselines are gaps in today's suite rather than differences from the design, and go to the report.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p11-011 to p11-036, p11-109 and p11-110 list the baselines, and p11-103 and p11-104 the gaps.

requirements.statement: The tests repo has exactly two targets, the deployed services and the docker-compose stack, one config file each, extending one shared config that holds the projects, the reporters, one retry and a trace on the first retry with a screenshot only on failure. One default project, chromium, runs every domain, and five opt-in projects run only when named: branded Chrome, Firefox, WebKit, an emulated iPhone 17 and an emulated Pixel 10. The four desktop projects render at 1280 by 1000 and the two mobile ones take their device's viewport. A deployed run gives each test 60 seconds and each expectation 15 seconds because each page load is a real network hop, a compose run keeps Playwright's defaults, and a test that needs longer sets its own through a helper that leaves a debug run untimed. Each flow step waits up to 30 seconds for its page's heading so a transient gateway error fails the step that hit it and names the page. Tests run fully in parallel, a run on CI refuses a test marked only, and how many browsers run at once is capped by a setting that takes a whole number or a percentage and stops the run with both accepted forms when it is anything else. Every run refuses to start against production, a missing service base URL or a domain with no base URL stops the run naming what was missing, a compose run from a workspace clone that does not own the stack stops before the first test unless told to carry on, a compose preflight fails fast when the animals frontend, backend or admin does not answer its health check, and a containerised compose run adds a host-resolver rule so the stack's localhost redirects resolve. Local service ports and deployed per-service subdomains are fixed; a laptop run against a deployed environment names the environment, and its back-end calls go through the protected gateway with a developer API key over the department's VPN; calls that leave the platform for the internet go through the platform proxy, while journey and service calls stay direct.
requirements.why: Any new end-to-end, accessibility or visual proof runs under these settings, and a change that needs a new route, port or longer budget has to be made here.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-025 to p16-033 and p16-068 to p16-078 give the configs, the projects, the timeouts, the retries and the guards; p16-060 to p16-067-m1 the addresses of every service on both targets; p16-197 the compose preflight and p16-152 the proxy rule.

requirements.statement: The tests repo is run by named scripts, one per suite and target, and by a profile on the deployed platform. Against the deployed services there are end-to-end, accessibility, Dynamics, cross-browser, BrowserStack, passive-security and active-security scripts, and against the compose stack end-to-end, accessibility, visual, cross-browser, BrowserStack, passive-security and active-security scripts plus a CI script for the workspace stack job; each excludes the type tags it does not run, and only the compose security scripts run the gate. Per-domain copies limit a run to that domain's own directory and are named to match the platform's profiles; a dash in the per-domain table means that domain has no specs of that test type yet. A deployed run picks its suite with a profile value, an unset profile running the default; a profile can be prefixed with a domain; a profile for a test type the domain has no specs of fails as no tests found, one whose directory does not exist stops the container naming the directory, and an unknown profile stops it listing every allowed value and domain, while the domain prefix never reaches the test runner. An active-security profile asked for on the deployed platform is refused, recorded in a failure marker and answered with a report page saying the profile only runs against the compose stack. A run that exits non-zero has its reason appended to that marker and the container exits 1 printing it; a security profile publishes the scan's report directory with the scan's own summary as its index and skips the Allure step, while every other profile publishes the Playwright report, copying it to the configured object store with a zip of its results, failing when the path is unset or the report is missing, and exiting with the publish step's code if publishing fails. A run can be narrowed with the runner's own parameters, and the report is opened or generated by its own commands.
requirements.why: A new suite, domain or test type has to be reachable by one of these scripts or profiles, and a chrome change that breaks a run shows up through this entrypoint.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-002-m1 to p16-024, p16-275 and p16-276 list the scripts and what each leaves out, and p16-135 to p16-151 with p16-136-m1 and p16-148-m1 the deployed profiles, their refusals and how each publishes its report.

requirements.statement: The tests repo holds end-to-end, accessibility and security tests for the animals frontend, its admin portal, the high-risk plants frontend and the INS front door with the address book, in four domains, each a functional area served by one or more services. A domain is selected by the directory its specs live in, which also gives them their base URL; a spec outside a known domain directory stops the run naming the four. Within a domain, specs are grouped as accessibility, end-to-end (with feature, page, journey and visual sub-folders) and security folders, but a folder only organises: the test type is selected by one of five tags and a suite is a domain's directory or one test type within it, each path ending in a slash because the runner reads it as a regular expression. A service tag is a different thing: it names a service whose pull request should also run the spec, whatever its test type or domain, and eight are recognised, each belonging to the domains that already run it by path. Linting fails a spec whose tags disagree with its test-type directory, and one that carries the service tag of a service whose pull request already runs its domain by path; the check asks the runner to list the tests so it reads the tags a test really has, names each offending test by file, line and title, and otherwise reports how many it checked. A further tag marks an end-to-end spec whose behaviour a frontend's own suite also proves.
requirements.why: A new spec has to sit in the right domain and carry the right tags, or the lint fails it and the pull-request runs either miss it or run it everywhere.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-079 to p16-092 give the domains, the folders, the five type tags, the eight service tags and the lint that enforces them; p16-001 the four services the suite covers.

requirements.statement: A spec in the tests repo is written to the suite's own conventions. It reaches a page through a named step in its domain's journey file rather than its own clicks, and a sequence two tests share becomes such a step with the local copies deleted; a flow or page object holds no assertion and an assertion two specs share lives in a shared checks module; a journey spec is never seeded, seeding being only for the set-up of a one-page assertion; test data is copied from real canned data and never invented, and a value that has a home is imported rather than retyped; answers are plain data apart from the steps that drive the pages, in named mandatory and full sets, and a spec starts from a set and overrides single values rather than changing the steps. A spec asserts which page is open through the page object's own URL pattern, opens a page on a trail through the page object, and never types a trail itself. Support code sits in named folders for specs, flows, page objects, domain constants, fixtures, adapters, canned data and cross-domain helpers, and shared code may not import a domain's page objects, flows or constants. A test title says what its assertions prove and a test must fail without the change it covers; a name predicts its return value and side effects and one concept has one name. A comment describes only the lines below it and only where a name cannot, the code carries no history, and a spec carries no ticket key, backlog or ruling id, release name or tracking wording in a comment, a title or a tag: the lint fails it and tells the author to say what the code does, or what the assertions prove, instead. A catch that drops its error is refused, as is an error or warning logged with only a string while a caught error is in scope; the lint also runs type-checked rules and refuses a floating promise. A test run is redirected to a file rather than piped. Lint, the formatting check and the type check run before a commit, with a pre-commit hook on the staged files.
requirements.why: Every new proof is reviewed against these rules, and the ban on ticket keys, release names and ruling ids in a spec is why a requirement's words have to say what the behaviour is rather than which decision produced it.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-209 to p16-229 give the lint rules and the code-quality conventions, p16-094, p16-094-m1 and p16-095 how a spec asserts a page and where a shared assertion lives, and p16-218 to p16-226 the folder layout and the answer sets.

requirements.statement: The tests repo's cross-browser set is existing end-to-end specs selected by one tag, with no specs of their own in the cross-browser folders, run in branded Chrome, the runner's Firefox and WebKit builds, an emulated iPhone 17 and an emulated Pixel 10, against the deployed services or the compose stack, one project at a time by naming the project with an equals sign and adding the tag filter, because a named project without it would run every test. On a hosted device service the tagged tests run in real Edge on Windows 11 and the runner's WebKit on the newest macOS, and a second tag selects short single-context flows for real Safari on the two current iOS versions, on an iPhone 18 Pro and an iPhone 17; a test keeps that tag only if it passes on both iPhones, and on a hosted run a test without its platform's tag is skipped naming the tag. A test is tagged only if it runs against the deployed services and renders a page the set does not already cover, chosen so that together the set renders as many pages as possible in each engine, preferring a journey walk and then one test per page the walks do not reach, and leaving out validation, back-end, visual, accessibility and security specs; a tagged test still runs in the default run. The animals and INS domains have cross-browser commands and the admin domain has none. Real Android browsers, real Firefox, real macOS Safari and Chrome on Windows and macOS are deliberately not covered, real Android being checked by hand before a release; branded Chrome ships only in the amd64 image. On the hosted service session reuse is off because a real iPhone allows one browser context, each run uses one session per processor up to the team limit, the local tunnel cannot open localhost from Safari or WebKit so those platforms run only against the deployed services, network logs and the service's own accessibility checking are off, credentials come only from the environment and a run stops before starting if either credential or every platform is missing; the hosted service is not run from GitHub Actions. On an iPhone user agent the accessible autocomplete adds a hidden position counter, so a spec must not assume a fixed viewport. The set is reviewed against the government's browser guidance when that list changes, a new iOS or macOS arrives, Windows 11 reaches end of support or the runner is upgraded.
requirements.why: A page that changes keeps or earns its cross-browser tag under these rules, and the shared chrome is what every tagged test renders.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-277 to p16-298 give the projects, the hosted platforms and their tags and rules, and what is deliberately left out; p16-171 to p16-193 how a test is chosen and run. The accessible autocomplete adds a hidden position counter on an iPhone user agent (repo-tests-p16-183).

requirements.statement: The tests repo's Dynamics integration checks, which prove a submitted notification reaches a domain's Dynamics instance through the Dataverse Web API, are not changed by this programme. They run only through their own profile, are left out of every other run, skip on the compose stack, read their settings by function rather than at load so one domain's missing setting cannot fail another's tests, fail at once naming a missing variable and never its value, and are given a longer base timeout; on the deployed platform their calls go through the platform proxy, which must allow the sign-in host and the Dynamics host.
requirements.why: Design and chrome changes reach no Dynamics field, so these checks are weighed where notification publishing is weighed, not here.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-153 to p16-162 describe the suite, its profile, its credentials and its timeouts as they stand.

requirements.statement: The tests repo's own build and delivery stand: a test image built on the official runner image with the London time zone, curl, zip, a Java runtime and the cloud CLI, dependencies installed from the lockfile with lifecycle scripts skipped, run as a non-root user, built for one architecture because of that CLI, and carrying a copied security-scanner install with the add-on that needs a browser profile removed. A push to the default branch builds and publishes the image to both registries, tagged with the computed next version and latest, labelled with the repo, the suite name, the build run and the commit, declared as a platform test suite run as a job, and commits the version tag; a pull request publishes a branch image through the workspace's branch-publish workflow with a layer cache the main publish writes. End-to-end tests run in continuous integration through the workspace's reusable workflow, which starts the workspace stack probing for the branch's images and runs the published test image against it, publishing reports; that workflow runs only for a pull request whose image publish succeeded or on manual dispatch with a branch to probe, keeps one run per branch, and reports a pending check and then the result back to the pull request. A pull request also runs the formatting check, the lint and the type check, and the same job runs weekly. The dependency audit is a separate job, so a newly published advisory does not gate the merge or block the pull request carrying the fix, and every allowlist entry must carry an advisory id, be active, give a reason and an owner and have a real expiry no more than three months away, an expired entry failing the check. The suite runs on its pinned runtime, is driven by its pinned test runner with the accessibility, reporting, device-service, database, queue and audit clients it declares, keeps non-secret settings in the platform's app config and credentials as platform secrets, clears its previous results and saved sessions at the start of a run, can seed a notification from a script of its own, documents the four workspace commands that start, build, stop and rebuild the stack, publishes its reports and cleans them up when a pull request closes, and is licensed under the Open Government Licence version 3 with its attribution kept.
requirements.why: A chrome change that breaks a run is caught by these checks, and an increment that adds a route or a fixture has to keep the image, the workflows and the audit green.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-194 to p16-208 give the image, the publishes and the workflows, p16-203 and p16-204 the audit's own rules, p16-264-m1 where settings and secrets live, and p16-265 to p16-271 the pinned runtime, dependencies, seeding script and stack commands.

requirements.statement: Documentation drift and housekeeping defects in the tests repo are not fixed by this programme: the run table that leaves out the two deployed security scripts; the accessibility documentation and the accessibility folder's README, which name no conformance standard, no viewport, no list of pages that must be scanned and no run command; the per-domain and profile tables that do not say whether the plants and admin domains' missing suites are planned or deliberately out of scope; the attacking plan's out-of-date note that the upload identifier is never reached; the security report's title, which names the animals service although the report covers six services; and the absence of any decisions ledger, so the only rulings the repo carries are the ones its prose states.
requirements.why: These are documentation and housekeeping defects in today's suite, not differences from the target design. They go to the report.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-012-m1, p16-272 to p16-274, p10-152, p11-072, p11-107 and p11-108 record the drift as it stands. The excluded-tag list, the runtime prerequisite and the exclusion table's selector names now agree with the code (repo-tests-p16-002-m1, p16-265, p15-132), so they are no longer listed.

requirements.statement: An end-to-end proof that creates an address or a transporter follows the suite's own rules for shared state. Every name it creates carries a timestamp or unique suffix so a search finds only that run's record, and the accessibility walks that add a transporter in parallel give it a name no other running test uses; the address-book fixtures delete every address and transporter they created when the test ends, pass or fail and on every retry, logging a failed delete with the record's id without failing the test; a transporter saved through the user interface is deleted only if the spec tracks it by name, and an address added on the add-address page or through the cross-service hand-off is not deleted at all. The shared journey addresses are seeded in global set-up through its own client so no test's clean-up removes them, and a spec that edits or deletes an address makes its own record instead; a record whose country is a name rather than a listed code is the one way, through the services alone, to copy an address the notification refuses. Because the book is shared and never wiped locally, a spec that counts rows searches for a token only its own run created or writes to an organisation whose book starts empty; because the picker lists records newest first and other workers are adding records, a spec that needs a record off page one creates enough newer records to fill page one and then follows Next until its record shows. On the deployed environments addresses expire about seven days after they are created where that is switched on, and the compose stack switches it off. A reset script brings a deployed environment's shared organisation back to a small known state, soft-deleting only records whose name matches a name a test creates, keeping the seeded journey addresses and the performance suite's records, run from a developer's own machine with their API key and never from continuous integration, reporting and deleting nothing by default, deleting addresses only when told to and transporters only when asked, printing the environment and organisation first, refusing production, and reporting in its dry run how many records it would delete and keep with the deletes by name and the commonest kept names.
requirements.why: The address book the navigation leads to is shared state that every worker reads, so a new proof has to create, name and clean up its records this way or it breaks other specs.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-035 to p16-044 and p16-246-m1 give the fixtures' clean-up and the shared-state rules, and p16-045 to p16-048 the reset script's own guards.

requirements.statement: How a commodity line is named and found in a test is weighed with the commodity pages, not here: the commodity page's tick-box label of scientific name then common name in brackets under a commodity-code heading, with the scientific name alone where reference data holds no common name; that one scientific name can sit under several commodity codes so a line is identified by code as well as name; that the aggregated notification's commodity label uses the first trade line's description; that the stack's reference-data stub answers only the searches saved from it, the first page of results holds 100 entries and only a species a search showed can be saved, so a seeded journey posts the search first; and that each line is named by search term, code, scientific name and common name, a spec building its expected label from that line or, where it needs the live answer, reading it through the reference-data client and handing it to the same helper.
requirements.why: These are the commodity pages' own content and the reference lists behind them, which the commodities area weighs against the target design and the data specification.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-049 to p16-052 and p16-051-m1 record the labels, the stub's limits and the line constants as they stand.

requirements.statement: What the end-to-end suite proves about one page's own content or one journey's own answers is weighed in that page's area, not here: that a brand-new notification opens at the origin page with nothing answered, the entry guard admits it on an answer the trader entered, and starting a notification answers origin and opens the overview; the arrival date's window and its unpadded display form and a temporary admission's later exit date; how an accompanying document is added and waited for, and the budgets its list and scan are given; the import reason's conditional purpose; the transporter pages' order, their add forms, where each save lands, and why two tests adding a transporter of the same name can refuse a list's save; the overview's two sets of task rows in their fixed order; the rail, cat and poultry consignments' own answers and where each walk ends; the permanent address page's place in the journey and the holding number answered on the consignment addresses page; what the animals API seed unlocks; a party picker's refusal of a record without the role, its server round trip and how a party's row and a summary card's links and subsections are found; how a species tick box and a transit port of exit are chosen; every named walk a spec starts from; and the admin portal's replay and delete banners that prove it is wired to the gateway.
requirements.why: This area stops at any one page's own content and answers; those pages' areas weigh the same behaviours against the target design and the data specification.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-232 to p16-262 and their missed claims record those pages' own behaviour and the suite's facts about them as they stand.

requirements.statement: A plants page that changes in the same increment as its animals twin is proved by the suites the plants domain has.
requirements.why: The owner's rule is that a change to something plants also has changes plants in the same increment, but the plants domain has end-to-end and visual specs only, so what counts as proof for a changed plants page is not settled.
requirements.deltaNote: The plants domain has compose scripts for end-to-end and visual only and none for accessibility or security (repo-tests-p16-018), a plants accessibility profile finds no tests (repo-tests-p16-138), and no attacking spec drives the plants journey (repo-tests-p11-105).

requirements.statement: The accessibility suite scans the INS front door and its address book: the blank address-type question, the blank add-address form, the add form fully entered with an optional second address line, a county and its roles ticked, an address's view page for a record with the required fields only and again for one with the extra fields, the edit form filled with a stored address, the delete confirmation, the address-type question, the add form and the edit form each with their error summary showing, the populated list and the list with the success banner after an address is added, the list's second page reached by seeding nine addresses and following Next, the dashboard in its default populated and sorted views, the not-found page, the dashboard with a search that matches a reference and again with one that matches nothing, the dashboard's paginated view where there is more than one page, the sign-in page on first load from a cold session and again with an error, with the sign-in stub's own error list excluded, and the unauthorised page. The address book's and the dashboard's longer pages are scanned again at both narrow viewports.
requirements.why: The INS front door and the address book are where the navigation leads, and every page that changes there must keep passing these scans.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p15-061 to p15-079 define the INS scans, the states each covers and the two narrow viewports.

requirements.statement: The tests repo's accessibility suite holds every scanned page, animals and INS alike, to WCAG 2.2 AA. Every test carries the @a11y tag and is reported under that standard, read from the fixture so the title and the rule set cannot drift apart, and every scan passes the five axe tags wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21a, wcag21aa and wcag22aa explicitly, because axe's own default leaves target-size out. A scan runs with axe's legacy mode off, so cross-origin iframes are scanned, and may be narrowed or widened per page with include, exclude and disabled rules. A scan waits for the DOM and then allows a bounded settling period, scanning anyway if that wait times out; it is recorded against the page's path; a test runs every one of its scans before failing and reports them together with each violation's severity, rule, description, node count, help link and first target, attaching them to the report as JSON; a failing scan fails its test and a test that takes the scan but never runs one fails too. The suite proves its own scanner on a real service page: with an unnamed button and two adjacent eight-pixel links injected, the scan reports button-name and target-size, and a test expected to fail is never retried. A test is allowed five minutes, and the accessibility runs use the same two configs as every other test type. Pages whose layout matters at small sizes are scanned again at 320 by 568, the reflow width, and at 568 by 320, for orientation and the reflow height, set for the whole test, and a narrow scan also proves the page does not scroll sideways once its tables are discounted, taking the same scan options as any other scan. A clean scan is not full conformance, and a state earns its own scan only where its value outweighs the set-up it needs.
requirements.why: Every page that changes must keep passing this suite, and a new scan has to be written to these rules.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p10-001 to p10-022 and p15-058 to p15-086-m2 define the suite and its narrow-viewport scans, and p10-142 to p10-144 with p15-080 and p15-081 prove the scanner catches a real fault.

requirements.statement: An accessibility scan leaves out only markup whose finding is an upstream disagreement in code the service does not own, and only the elements that carry it, never a page or a rule as a whole: the origin page's region-of-origin-code radio and the import reason page's radios that open a conditional reveal, because govuk-frontend sets aria-expanded on such a radio and axe's aria-allowed-attr rule rejects it; the accompanying documents page's file upload button, in every state of that page and at both narrow viewports, because axe's label-content-name-mismatch rule joins the button's status text and its Choose file text without a space while the browser's accessible name contains the visible text and so meets Label in Name; and, on the INS sign-in page with an error, the sign-in stub's own error list. The file upload button exclusion is deleted once a release of axe or govuk-frontend no longer reports the finding. The three journey exclusions are kept in one shared module, which the accessibility documentation names, and no INS scan uses them.
requirements.why: Every page this work changes keeps being scanned whole apart from these elements, and a new exclusion has to meet the same bar.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p10-013 to p10-017, p10-153 to p10-157, p15-131 to p15-133 and p16-299 to p16-300 give the shared exclusions and their reasons; p15-078 the INS sign-in stub exclusion.

requirements.statement: The accessibility suite walks the live-animals journey from the notification list to the declaration and scans every journey page as it first opens: the list, the origin page, the overview with only origin answered, the commodity selection and details pages, the identification page, the import reason page, the additional details page, the upload documents page, the consignment addresses page, the consignor picker, the holding number page, the arrival details page, the transit countries page, the transporter list, the transporter type question, the commercial transporter form, the review page through the journey's own review step, and the declaration unticked. It walks the journey again filling each page in, from a notification already started, and scans each page with its answers on it, the upload documents page both filled and with its saved document scanned, the consignment addresses page with all five parties, the transporter list again after a new transporter is saved, the declaration ticked and the submitted confirmation. Each page is reached through the journey flow's own steps and page objects rather than by the spec's own navigation.
requirements.why: This is the existing end-to-end accessibility proof of the journey. Each page the target design changes must still pass it, and a page added or moved changes the flow step once for the whole suite.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p10-023 and p10-044 define the two walks, p10-024 to p10-065 and p10-159 the pages and states each scans, and p10-145 how a spec reaches them.

requirements.statement: The accessibility suite walks the live-animals journey a third time, from a brand-new notification at the origin page, and scans every page that validates input while its errors are on screen, a scan running only once the error summary headed 'There is a problem' is visible: the origin page, the commodity selection and details pages, the draft review refused with sections unfinished, the identification page with an over-long ear tag, the import reason page without a purpose, the upload documents page empty, with a restricted file type, with an oversize file, with an infected file and again once that file is removed, the holding number page, the arrival details page with a past date, the transit countries page with no country chosen, the transporter list with none chosen, the transporter type question with neither chosen, both transporter forms refused, and the declaration unticked. The consignment addresses page, the party pickers and the review on the way to the declaration are passed without a scan in this walk.
requirements.why: This is the existing accessibility proof of the shared error summary and inline errors on journey pages.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p10-066 and p10-067 define the walk and the wait, p10-068 to p10-086 the error states it scans, and p10-160 to p10-162 where it starts and what it passes unscanned.

requirements.statement: The accessibility suite also scans the rest of the animals service: the import reason page with Transit and with Temporary admission of horses revealed, the transporter type question with Private chosen and the private transporter form empty, refused and filled; the commodity details page with two species and the identification page empty and filled with the horse and cat identifier sets; the review refused, the overview complete, the consignment addresses page, the identification page, the review during an amendment and the upload documents page with a scanned document, at both narrow viewports, from seeded drafts; the notification list in its default, sorted, searched, empty-result and paged views and at both narrow viewports, and the not-found page; the review for an unlocked draft and refused, the overview with every task complete, the read-only submitted view and the submission confirmation; the overview and view during an amendment, the cancel-amendment confirmation and its success banner, the delete confirmation and the list's deleted banner; the consignment addresses page with its Change and Edit details links, and the consignor edit page filled and refused; and the unauthorised page from a cold start.
requirements.why: This is the existing accessibility proof of the rest of the animals service; each of these pages keeps passing it as it changes.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p10-087 to p10-141 and p10-163 to p10-164, with p10-087-m1 and p10-089-m1, define the scans.

requirements.statement: Gaps in today's accessibility proof are not closed by this programme. On the animals side no scan covers the permanent address page, four of the five party pickers, four of the five party edit pages, the sign-in page or the organisation picker, or the hand-off from a party picker to the address book's add-address page, and the narrow-viewport scan of the notification list does not check for sideways scrolling; the journey has no contact address page left to scan. On the INS side the empty dashboard, the empty address book and the address book's load-failure state are deliberately left unscanned, and the notification type page and every transporter page go unscanned.
requirements.why: These are coverage gaps in today's suites, not differences from the target design. They go to the report.

requirements.statement: The accessibility suite scans the germinal-products set's journey pages, from specs under the animals domain's accessibility folder in a germinal-products sub-folder, run by the existing animals project with no project of its own and written to the same rules as the live-animals scans.
requirements.why: The germinal-products set is a new sibling set whose specs the owner placed in the animals project's accessibility folder, and accessibility is a constraint every page must meet; today no scan reaches the set.
requirements.deltaNote: Every accessibility spec walks the live-animals journey only, and the only set root any of them names is live animals (repo-tests-p10-151).

requirements.statement: The tests repo's security suite is a traffic-driven OWASP ZAP scan of six services, each its own named ZAP context with its own address from its own setting: the animals frontend, the animals admin, the INS frontend, the animals backend, the plants backend and the address book. Playwright drives real signed-in journeys through the proxy rather than letting ZAP crawl, so coverage is traffic-driven and the attacking corpus is curated by hand; the three APIs are scanned because every API client inherits the run's proxy. There are two profiles: a passive one that runs the end-to-end suite without the attacking specs and is safe against a deployed environment, and an attacking one that runs only the @active corpus, runs on the compose stack and in a weekday scheduled GitHub Action whose password-protected report is pruned after seven days, and is refused on the deployed platform because its journeys delete records the scan then re-fires with fuzzed payloads. Anything but the exact attacking profile name is treated as passive. Identifiers in a page or API address are declared to ZAP as data rather than structure, from a context plan registered before any traffic exists; all three plans must declare the same contexts; diagnostics are excluded rather than scanned; the DOM cross-site-scripting rule is off; the sign-in stub is observed but never attacked while the service's own sign-in handlers are in scope; and the uploader and the queue-consuming INS backend are out of scope with their reasons. A run fails on a FAIL-rated alert from the rules file (an unlisted alert failing only if it is high risk, and no alert ignored today), on a plan error or a plan running past five hours, on a scan that finished at or within half a minute of its 60-minute cap, or, in the attacking profile, on a declared context that saw no traffic; a per-domain run gates only that domain's contexts and is labelled scoped, the full run being the authoritative clean bill of health, and an unknown domain is refused by name. ZAP listens on a loopback port outside the workspace's port ranges with a local default key, runs as a container beside the stack locally and as an in-process daemon pointed at each per-service subdomain on the deployed platform, using the same plans and gate. Each run clears its report folder but never removes it, writes a landing page before failing with a row per site, its request count and alert counts and notices for a cut-short, partial or scoped run, publishes ZAP's log and machine-readable report as HTML with the whole Playwright report beside it, and never runs the gate against a spec run that failed or refused to start.
requirements.why: Every route that is added or changed must be driven through this scan to be attacked, and a new spec has to be written to these rules.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p11-037 to p11-102, p15-094 to p15-115 and p16-106 to p16-134 define the suite, its profiles, its contexts and its failure conditions; p16-144 to p16-148 give how a deployed run starts ZAP itself and publishes its report.

requirements.statement: The attacking corpus drives through the proxy: the animals sign-in round trip with a refused user and a sign-out, from a cold start; a whole submitted live-animals journey to its confirmation; the reason-gated pages for Transit and Temporary admission of horses with additional details saved and returned from the overview, and a private transporter typed by hand; amend and copy as new, then cancel amendment and delete; a document upload waited through its scan and then opened; a draft validation error on the origin page; the notification list's search, paging and sorting; the review page's Change trail; the INS address book's whole record lifecycle with a role-filtered tab and the dashboard opened at the end; the add page's cross-service hand-off parameters, of which only the refused side is proven; and the INS sign-in round trip, which holds the suite's only check that the INS front door renders its 'Log out' link.
requirements.why: A page or route that changes keeps being attacked only while a spec in this corpus still drives it, so a change to any of these journeys updates the spec that drives it.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p11-087 to p11-095 and p11-112 to p11-115 give the animals and INS attacking specs, p15-098 to p15-106 and p16-125 to p16-127 the INS ones in detail.

requirements.statement: Gaps in today's security scan are not closed by this programme. No attacking spec drives the high-risk plants journey, so the plants backend is a declared context that nothing reaches and a full attacking run cannot pass the no-traffic gate as things stand; only a per-domain run avoids it. No transporter route is driven through the proxy. Only the refused side of the address book's cross-service hand-off is in scope, because no accepted token can be seeded.
requirements.why: These are coverage gaps in today's suite, not differences from the target design. They go to the report.

requirements.statement: The attacking corpus drives a germinal-products notification journey through the proxy, from specs under the animals domain's security folder in a germinal-products sub-folder, run by the existing animals project, so the germinal set's pages and identifiers on the animals frontend are attacked as the live-animals ones are.
requirements.why: Security coverage is traffic-driven, so a germinal page no spec drives is invisible to the scan; the owner placed the germinal set's security specs in the animals project's security folder.
requirements.deltaNote: The only submitted journey the attacking corpus drives is the live-animals one (repo-tests-p11-088), and a route no spec drives is invisible to the scan (repo-tests-p11-038).

requirements.statement: The tests repo signs each worker in once per domain and its tests restore that session, the saved state holding only the auth cookie and never written until a fresh context has proved it restores to a signed-in landing page; sign-in waits for the landing page or the sign-in failure page before deciding to try again. A spec that must start unauthenticated opts out with a cold-start state, a spec that needs the same user in a new session carries only the auth cookie into a new context, and session reuse can be switched off, which caps the deployed run's workers. Reuse was proved against one deployed environment by a probe that mints one session and reuses it across twenty fresh contexts, refuses to run against production, and is to be re-run before relying on reuse elsewhere. The suite signs in as two stub identities mirroring the sign-in stub's data, a default single-organisation user and a second user with two organisations for organisation choice; the password comes from the environment with a local stub default and is never written into a trace, the sign-in fixtures have their own longer timeout, and no spec wipes the database because every spec creates the state it asserts on.
requirements.why: Any new end-to-end proof of sign-in or navigation has to work within these existing suite rules.
requirements.deltaNote: repo-tests-p16-053 to p16-059 give the session rules, p16-163 to p16-167 the identities and password handling, p16-034 the sign-in retry and p16-093 that nothing is wiped.

conflicts.about: What proves a plants page this programme changes, given the plants domain has end-to-end and visual specs only and no accessibility or security specs.

positions.says: Where plants has the same page or behaviour, the same increment changes plants too.
The plants domain has docker-compose scripts for end-to-end and visual only, and none for accessibility or security.
A plants accessibility profile on the deployed platform fails with no tests found.
No attacking spec exists for the high-risk plants journey, so the plants backend is declared as a context with an attack job of its own that nothing drives.
Neither the per-domain script table nor the profile table says whether plants' missing accessibility and security suites are planned or deliberately out of scope.

conflicts.outcome: Nothing ranks the two readings. The owner's rule that plants takes the same change in the same increment can be read as carrying the animals proof across, which would mean writing plants an accessibility suite and a security corpus, or as carrying only the change, which leaves a changed plants page proved by the end-to-end and visual specs it has. Unlike the germinal-products set, whose accessibility and security specs a ruling places in the animals project, no ruling and none of the tests repo's own documentation settles it for plants, so it goes to the owner with a default.
conflicts.question: When an increment changes a plants page as well as an animals one, does plants get accessibility and security specs for that page, or is its end-to-end and visual proof enough?
conflicts.default: Animals and INS pages keep their existing accessibility and security suites. A plants page that changes is proved by the plants domain's end-to-end and visual specs and by the plants frontend's own in-repo checks, and no plants accessibility specs or attacking security specs are written; the full attacking run keeps failing its no-traffic gate on the plants backend context, so only per-domain attacking runs are used, and that gap goes to the report.
